data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is primarily driven by the slow release of stored sensible heat from urban thermal mass, and the cross-city magnitude of this effect scales directly with city size because larger cities contain a greater absolute volume of heat-storing masonry and asphalt that intercepts daytime solar radiation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If urban materials have high albedo and low thermal mass, the heat storage release would be insufficient to account for the nocturnal temperature gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural thermal mass (e.g., dense vegetation or soil moisture) approaches urban thermal mass, the differential cooling rate would diminish.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If city size increases without a corresponding increase in dense urban materials (e.g., sprawling low-density suburbs), the scaling relationship fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, high-thermal-capacity materials like concrete and asphalt absorb solar energy. After sunset, while rural areas cool rapidly via radiative loss, the urban fabric releases this stored sensible heat into the canopy air, maintaining warmer temperatures. The magnitude of this effect increases in larger cities simply due to the proportional aggregation of heat storage volume relative to surrounding rural areas.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
